Field surveys conducted in the high-elevation streams of the Zagros Mountains reveal that adult female Yellow-spotted newts attain a remarkable ultimate snout-vent length of 6.34 cm [Li = 6.34 cm], though measurements from a broader population sample indicate a range spanning from 5.66 to 7.03 cm (5.66-7.03 cm) [Li = 5.66-7.03 cm]. Males of this species reach a corresponding ultimate snout-vent length of 6.38 cm [Li = 6.38 cm], a value derived from the maximum recorded length for males as illustrated in published growth figures. This subtle sexual size dimorphism, with females averaging slightly shorter than the male maximum, is consistent with patterns observed in other members of the genus Neurergus, where the demands of egg production often select for larger female body cavities, yet here the disparity remains modest. The stream-dwelling salamanders are highly dependent on cool, clear water for their aquatic larval phase, and the available morphometric data underline the importance of preserving these habitats to maintain the full range of adult body sizes observed in the wild.

Reproductive output in Neurergus crocatus has been quantified through controlled laboratory observations at a constant water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], where females deposit their eggs in distinct clusters containing between 20 and 40 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 20 and 40 eggs per clutch]. Under these stable thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the number of clutches produced annually, reaches approximately 1.2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 clutches per year], translating to a substantial total of around 120 eggs deposited over the course of a single breeding season. This intermittent egg-laying strategy, where multiple discrete clutches are spaced across several weeks, is a common adaptation among montane salamanders and likely allows females to spread the energetic burden of reproduction across the brief spring window when stream temperatures are optimal for embryonic development.

The neonatal stage of the Yellow-spotted newt begins with the eclosion of the aquatic larva from the gelatinous egg mass, a process that occurs after an incubation period of 45 days [ab = 45 days] when eggs are maintained at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Upon hatching from a yolk-laden egg measuring roughly 2 mm in diameter, the newly emerged endotrophic larva carries a minimal wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume of the egg. This diminutive mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the yolk-sac larva, which relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first weeks of life. The protracted incubation period at this relatively cool temperature is typical for salamanders breeding in headwater streams, where low metabolic rates during embryogenesis promote extended developmental times but also reduce the risk of premature hatching in an environment where prey availability for exotrophic tadpoles may be seasonally pulsed.

Growth from the tiny endotrophic hatchling to a reproductively viable adult is a trajectory that culminates in a substantial ultimate wet weight at birth of 8.87 grams [Wwi = 8.87 grams], a value estimated based on allometric scaling relationships derived from the congeneric species Neurergus microspilotus. This remarkable increase in body mass, representing a more than two-thousand-fold gain over the 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] recorded at hatching, underscores the intense feeding activity of the free-swimming larva and the growing juvenile during the aquatic tadpole and terrestrial juvenile stages. The post-metamorphic juvenile, or eft, forages actively on stream invertebrates to fuel this rapid mass accumulation. Attaining this adult body mass is a prerequisite for the successful onset of gonadal maturation, as individuals must first meet the energetic demands of a large body size before investing in gamete production.

Sexual maturation in Neurergus crocatus is a delayed process, with puberty occurring at 4 years since birth [tp = 4 years since birth] when newts are maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] in captivity. This 4-year interval from the hatching event to the onset of gonadal activity represents a significant investment in somatic growth before reproductive effort begins. The overall lifespan of the species is similarly extended under these cool thermal conditions, with the maximum recorded longevity reaching 13 years [am = 13 years] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of the Salamandridae. This combination of delayed maturity and substantial longevity is characteristic of slow-paced life histories typical of high-elevation amphibians, where seasonal constraints on activity and reproduction impose a premium on adult survival and iteroparous breeding across multiple seasons.
